entry.title: How this garden works
entry.content:
A blog is a stream. You publish a post, it scrolls away, and the version you shipped on a Tuesday is the version that stands forever. That works for announcements. It works badly for the things I actually want to keep here: a poem that is not finished, a grammar pattern I half understand, an argument I am still losing to myself.

So this is a garden instead. Notes get planted small and are tended when I have something to add. Nothing here claims to be finished, and the ones that are finished say so.

The beds

Every note grows in exactly one bed, and the strip at the top of the garden switches between them.

tech is the engineering work — embedded systems, robotics, the things that cost me an afternoon and should not cost me another one. poetry is verse. music is songs I have covered. language is what I am learning in Spanish, English, German, and whatever comes next. philosophy is the longer arguments. misc is everything that refuses to sit in the other five, including this note.

Tags cut across the beds. A note about the rhythm of a German poem is tagged german whether it grew in the language bed or the poetry one, and the tag page collects both.

The badges

Next to a note’s title there is a small badge saying how grown it is. It is the most useful thing on the page, because it tells you how much to trust what you are reading.

A seedling was just planted. It is rough, probably incomplete, and quite likely wrong in places — I put it up because writing it down badly beats not writing it down. A budding note has been back a few times; the idea holds, the edges do not. An evergreen note has been tended often enough that I am willing to stand behind it. This one is evergreen.

Notes move between stages in one direction, slowly, and a seedling that never becomes anything is allowed to stay a seedling.

Planted and tended

Dates here work differently than on a blog. Planted is when a note first went up. Last tended is the last time I touched it and thought it was better afterwards. A note from two years ago that was tended last week is more current than one planted last month and abandoned — the dates are there so you can tell which is which.

How verse is set

Poems keep their line breaks exactly as typed, which sounds obvious and is not. Markdown collapses a single newline into a space, so a stanza pasted into an ordinary paragraph comes out as one long run-on line — which is why so many sites resort to trailing double-spaces or raw <br> tags to hold verse together.

The apparition of these faces in the crowd; Petals on a wet, black bough.

— Ezra Pound, In a Station of the Metro (1913)

The stanza above is marked with {: .poem} on the line immediately after it. That one marker gives it the serif face, the roomier leading, the stem down the left, and the preserved line breaks. Ordinary prose needs nothing and behaves normally.

The rest of the machinery

Song covers embed from YouTube through a small include that takes the bare video id, sizes the player from CSS so it fills the column at the right shape, and loads it from the no-cookie domain so nothing is set on you until you press play.

Comments are on, behind a button. Nothing is requested from a third party — no frame, no script, no cookie — until you ask for the thread. If you never click, the page never talks to anyone but this site.

Animated GIFs are served as they are rather than through the image pipeline that generates responsive WebP for the photographs, because resizing an animated GIF without coalescing its frames first is a reliable way to turn it into a still.

Where to start

If you came for the engineering, the tech bed is the one you want. If you came for something else, the strip at the top of the garden is the whole map.

Nothing here is finished. That is the point.
entry.summary: Why this section is a garden instead of a blog, what the beds and the badges mean, and how the notes here are meant to be read.

entry.title: What grows in the philosophy bed

link.title: What grows in the philosophy bed

entry.content:
Questions I keep turning over, written out properly enough that I can find the flaw in them.

I am not a philosopher and these are not papers. They are the long-form version of an argument I have been having with myself — mostly about work, about what technology is actually for, and about what a good life looks like from inside an engineering career.

Writing an argument down is the fastest way to discover that it does not hold. Some notes here will end with me less certain than I started, which I have decided to treat as the point rather than a failure.

Expect this bed to move slowly. An essay that makes it to evergreen has survived me disagreeing with it at least twice.
entry.summary: Questions I keep turning over, written out properly enough that the flaws in them become findable.

entry.title: What grows in the language bed

link.title: What grows in the language bed

entry.content:
Spanish is my first language. English I use every working day. German I am still climbing — around A2, which is far enough to order breakfast and nowhere near far enough to argue.

This bed is where the climbing gets written down: grammar that only clicked on a second pass, words that refuse to stay learned, sentences I found in the wild and had to take apart to see what was holding them up.

The convention here is that the first tag on a note is the language itself, so everything about German ends up collected on one page whether it started life as a grammar note or as a poem I was trying to read without help.

These are written for me first. If they are useful to someone climbing the same hill, so much the better.
entry.summary: Grammar that took a second pass to click, words that refuse to stay learned, and sentences found in the wild and taken apart.

entry.title: What grows in the music bed

link.title: What grows in the music bed

entry.content:
Songs I have borrowed for a while.

Covers go here: usually a video take, sometimes only an audio file when the recording is rougher than the playing. Where a song is in neither Spanish nor English, I will often set the original lyrics beside my own translation — which is the point where this bed quietly turns into the language one.

These are not performances and I make no claim to be a trained musician. They are closer to reading something aloud: a way of paying proper attention to a piece of music I like, and finding out what is actually inside it once you have to play every part yourself.
entry.summary: Songs I have borrowed for a while — covers, the occasional rough take, and lyrics set beside their translation.

entry.title: What grows in the poetry bed

link.title: What grows in the poetry bed

entry.content:
An engineering portfolio is an odd place to keep poems. I decided that was a reason to do it rather than a reason not to.

This bed is for verse: mine, and now and then lines by someone else that I want to keep somewhere I will actually run into them again. Poems here are rarely finished, which is what the maturity badge is for — a seedling is a draft I am still arguing with.

The one technical thing worth saying is that this site holds line breaks exactly as they were typed. That matters more for verse than for anything else here, and it is the reason a poem can sit in the same place as everything else without being flattened into a paragraph.

The bed is empty as I plant this note. That is the honest state of it, and it will change.
entry.summary: Why verse lives on the same site as firmware notes, and what to expect from the poems kept here.

entry.title: What grows in the tech bed

link.title: What grows in the tech bed

entry.content:
This is the working notebook: embedded systems, robotics, and the parts of both that only reveal themselves on real hardware.

Most of what lands here starts as something that cost me an afternoon — a scheduling assumption that was wrong, a frame that decoded fine on the bench and not in the vehicle, a build that only failed on the target. Writing it down is cheaper than paying for it twice, and a note is easier to search than my memory is.

Expect notes at different stages of certainty. A seedling here is often a hypothesis I have not finished testing, so check the badge before you trust a conclusion.

If you arrived from my projects, those are finished things with a result to show. This is the other half: the reasoning, the dead ends, and the parts that never make it into a README.
entry.summary: The working notebook — embedded systems, robotics, and the parts of both that only show themselves on real hardware.
